Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette:
Ibrahim, a 64-year-old politician, sat in the softly lit office of his therapist, his hands clasped tightly in his lap. As a relief worker in a war zone years ago, he had witnessed horrors that many could only imagine. The memories, however, were not mere recollections; they were visceral and terrifying, emerging uninvited and demanding his attention when he least expected it. The moment he had stepped into that ravaged town, he had felt the weight of despair pressing down on him like a physical force. He recalled the acrid smell of burnt debris, mingled with the scent of fear and loss. That smell haunted him still, a powerful olfactory cue that transported him back to the chaos of gunfire and sirens, where he had felt utterly powerless.

Since then, Ibrahim had become increasingly vigilant and hyper-aware of his surroundings. He often found himself scanning the streets for signs of danger, even in safe environments. A lingering silence in a room would send a shiver down his spine, prompting him to brace for an impending catastrophe. He had learned to take precautions, checking the locks on doors and windows multiple times before settling down for the night. It was a ritual he could not shake, a behavior rooted in the belief that if he could control his environment, he could protect himself from the threats that lurked in the shadows of his mind.

Interactions with strangers had become fraught with anxiety. When someone approached him, especially during public events or political gatherings, a sense of dread would wash over him. He felt as though they were probing into his psyche, unearthing buried fears. Conversations about military topics were particularly triggering. He would freeze internally, his heart racing, as others shared their opinions or experiences related to conflict. He tried hard to maintain a facade of composure, forcing himself to control his emotions, but it often felt like a losing battle. The effort to appear unbothered left him emotionally exhausted, and he would retreat into himself, seeking distractions to fill the void.

Work had become a refuge and a prison for Ibrahim. He threw himself into his political duties, believing that if he could stay busy, he could keep the memories at bay. Yet, the more he worked, the more isolated he felt. Days turned into weeks, and he often found himself in the office late into the night, the soft hum of the fluorescent lights drowning out his chaotic thoughts. Colleagues noticed his absence in social gatherings; his once vibrant interactions had dwindled to hollow exchanges. A sense of despair gnawed at him for losing touch with the very people he had once inspired.

The fragmented pieces of his memories began to surface more frequently, each time more disjointed than the last. He would recall the faces of those he couldn’t save, images flashing in and out of focus like a broken film reel. Each recollection brought forth an overwhelming wave of terror that he could hardly bear. He often had to stop what he was doing, his heart racing and breath catching in his throat, as the emotional tide threatened to drown him. Ibrahim had come to believe that these memories were a reflection of his failure to protect those who needed him most. The guilt intertwined with his grief, amplifying his need to control every aspect of his life.

As he sat in the therapist's office, Ibrahim felt a mix of trepidation and hope. The weight of his symptoms had grown unbearable; he could no longer ignore the toll they were taking on his life. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never reclaim the man he once was, that the shadows of his past would forever cloud his future. Yet, deep down, he yearned for a release from the chains of his memories, a chance to find peace amidst the chaos of his thoughts. Seeking help had been a step of courage, a recognition that perhaps he did not have to face his demons alone. As he took a deep breath, he wondered if it was finally time to confront the shadows that had haunted him for far too long.
